Family Health

Trichomoniasis: symptoms, tests and partner care

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Trichomoniasis, often called trich, is a common and treatable sexually transmitted infection caused by the parasite Trichomonas vaginalis. Many people feel completely well while carrying it. If you have new genital symptoms or a partner has a positive result, a sexual-health assessment can help you get the right treatment and reduce the chance of passing it back and forth.

An infection can be present without symptoms

Most people with trichomoniasis have few or no symptoms. When symptoms occur, they may appear about five to twenty-eight days after exposure, start much later, or come and go. Feeling well is therefore not a reliable way to decide whether testing or partner treatment is needed.

Without treatment, infection may persist for months or years. A test result cannot usually establish the exact date it was acquired or prove that a partner recently had sex with someone else. The immediate priorities are care, a clear follow-up plan and respectful communication.

Vaginal and urinary symptoms can vary

Possible symptoms include itching, burning, redness, swelling or soreness around the genitals. Vaginal discharge may increase or change in smell, colour or texture; it can be yellow-green, thin or frothy, but not everyone has the same appearance. Urination or vaginal sex may feel painful.

Report spotting, unexpected vaginal bleeding, urinary frequency or abdominal discomfort as well. These can have other explanations, so do not diagnose trichomoniasis from a discharge colour, photograph or symptom checklist. Bacterial vaginosis, thrush and other infections can overlap or occur at the same time.

Symptoms in people with a penis also need attention

Trichomoniasis may cause discharge from the penis, irritation inside it, burning when urinating or after ejaculation, or a frequent need to urinate. Many affected people have no symptoms at all.

The urethra is a common site, but it is too absolute to say the infection can affect only that structure. Associated inflammation can involve the prostate or other genital structures. Pain or swelling should be assessed rather than assumed to be an uncomplicated infection; sudden severe testicular pain needs emergency care.

How the parasite is passed between partners

Transmission mainly involves sexual contact with infected genital fluids, including penis-to-vagina or vagina-to-vagina contact. Shared sex toys can also transfer infection. A person does not need visible discharge or irritation to pass it on.

Ordinary contact such as hugging, sharing food or sitting on a toilet seat is not a usual route. Infection outside the genital area is uncommon, but this should not become a blanket promise that every activity without vaginal penetration is risk-free. Discuss the type of contact with a clinician when deciding what testing is appropriate.

Risk is about exposure, not a judgment about someone

Sex without a condom, multiple or new partners, a previous STI and a previous episode of trichomoniasis can increase the likelihood of exposure or reinfection. Someone in a long-term relationship can still have an infection that went unnoticed earlier.

Trichomoniasis is not limited to young adults; older women can also be affected. Population estimates depend on place, age group and how testing was done. Those averages should not decide whether an individual with symptoms or an affected partner deserves assessment.

An appointment and a suitable sample establish the next step

A doctor or nurse will ask about symptoms, possible exposure, previous treatment and pregnancy possibilities. They may examine the genital area and collect a vaginal or urethral swab, or request urine. Some services offer a self-collected vaginal swab.

You can ask for an explanation, a chaperone or a pause during an examination. Testing may also include HIV, syphilis, gonorrhoea and chlamydia. An ordinary urine test or a previous STI screen does not necessarily mean trichomoniasis was included; ask which infections are being checked.

Different laboratory tests have different limits

Molecular tests detect the parasite’s genetic material and are generally more sensitive than examining a fresh sample under a microscope. Depending on the service and specimen, an antigen test or culture may also be used. The laboratory must use a test suitable for that sample and patient.

A negative microscope examination does not reliably exclude infection when suspicion remains. Likewise, an incidental mention of trichomonas on a cervical screening report is not a confirmed diagnosis by itself; a suitable diagnostic test is needed. Ask when results will arrive and what to do if symptoms continue.

Prescribed oral treatment usually clears the infection

Medicines such as metronidazole act against this parasite. Tinidazole is an alternative in some circumstances. The prescriber chooses the medicine and course according to the person, local guidance, pregnancy, allergies and any previous treatment. A single dose and a multiday course are not interchangeable instructions.

Complete the course exactly as prescribed even when symptoms improve. Vaginal metronidazole gel, ordinary thrush treatments and home remedies are not substitutes for the recommended oral treatment. If you miss or vomit a dose, have troublesome side effects or suspect an allergy, ask the prescriber or pharmacist what to do rather than doubling up.

Check alcohol and other medicine precautions

Tell the pharmacist about other prescriptions, nonprescription medicines and supplements. Follow the leaflet for the product supplied, including alcohol precautions. For example, NHS advice for oral metronidazole is to avoid alcohol during treatment and for two days afterward; MedlinePlus advises three days after tinidazole.

Do not assume that waiting twenty-four hours is enough or use generic advice to override your own instructions. If the clinic and label seem to disagree, ask them to clarify before drinking. Keep the treatment course intact while getting advice about nausea, vomiting or other side effects.

Treat partners even when they feel well

Current partners generally need treatment for trichomoniasis even if they have no symptoms or are waiting for a result. A clinic can help identify which recent partners should be contacted and can offer confidential notification. Each person needs an appropriate prescription; sharing one course can leave both inadequately treated.

Avoid sex while either person is being treated. Wait until everyone has finished treatment, symptoms have resolved and the clinic’s advised waiting period has passed. NHS patient advice is to wait at least one week after all partners finish. Condoms reduce future risk but do not replace completing this treatment period.

Recovery and repeat testing are separate questions

Symptoms often begin improving within a few days, but there is no guarantee that every infection or symptom disappears within one week. Contact the clinic if symptoms persist, return or worsen. A repeat problem may reflect reinfection, missed doses, a different condition or, less commonly, drug resistance.

For sexually active women, CDC recommends repeat testing around three months after treatment because reinfection is common, even when partners were treated. Evidence for routine retesting of men is less clear; persistent symptoms or further exposure still need review. Agree on follow-up before the appointment ends.

A test taken too early can mislead

Testing persistent symptoms is different from the routine three-month check. A molecular test can detect leftover genetic material after the living parasite has been cleared. CDC advises that this type of test should not be used before three weeks after treatment finishes when assessing persistence.

That timing does not mean you must wait three weeks to contact the clinic about pain, ongoing symptoms or possible reinfection. The clinician can assess you now and choose an appropriate test or plan. Repeated treatment failure may require specialist advice rather than repeatedly taking leftover tablets.

Other infections and complications deserve their own assessment

Genital inflammation is associated with an increased chance of acquiring HIV, and trichomoniasis can coexist with other infections. A positive trichomoniasis result does not mean you have HIV; appropriate testing and prevention advice are separate parts of care.

Pelvic inflammatory disease affects the upper reproductive organs and can lead to scarring, ongoing pain, fertility problems or ectopic pregnancy. These are possible complications, not an inevitable consequence of every trich infection. Significant pelvic pain, fever, unusual bleeding or feeling unwell needs prompt assessment; severe pain, heavy bleeding, fainting or collapse needs emergency care.

Pregnancy and breastfeeding change the prescribing discussion

Trichomoniasis in pregnancy is associated with early birth, early rupture of membranes and babies who are small or have a low birth weight. Transmission around birth is uncommon but possible. These risks do not mean a complication is certain, and treatment cannot promise to prevent every adverse outcome.

Symptomatic pregnant people should be assessed and treated at any stage of pregnancy. Appropriately prescribed metronidazole is considered low risk; tinidazole should be avoided in pregnancy because safety evidence is limited. Tell the clinician if you are breastfeeding too, because advice depends on the medicine and regimen. Do not stop feeding or start leftover medicine without a specific plan.

Reduce future exposure and keep care accessible

Use external or internal condoms correctly and consistently. Avoid sharing sex toys; if shared, clean them according to their instructions and use a new condom between users where appropriate. Avoid vaginal douching, which does not remove the infection and can increase irritation or infection risk.

Avoiding sexual exposure prevents sexually acquired infection. If you are sexually active, testing, agreed relationship boundaries and open discussion of STI results can lower risk. Ask your clinic which screening schedule fits your circumstances. Treatment does not provide immunity, so a new exposure or recurring symptom deserves another conversation.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

CDC and WHO guidance support appropriate testing, prescribed oral treatment and coordinated partner care. Local regimens and advice can differ.

Routine reinfection testing and testing persistent symptoms have different purposes and timing. Pregnancy requires a medicine-specific decision rather than reassurance that all options are equally safe.

How BeMama can help

Keep your treatment dates, questions and follow-up appointment in one place if helpful. A general symptom record cannot confirm an STI, notify partners or replace a confidential clinical visit.

When to seek help

Seek urgent assessment for significant pelvic pain or fever, especially if pregnancy is possible. Severe pain, heavy bleeding, fainting, collapse or sudden severe testicular pain requires emergency care.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Trichomoniasis is treatable and can be present without symptoms.
  • A suitable laboratory test is more reliable than guessing from discharge.
  • Complete prescribed treatment and include partner care.
  • Ask about repeat-test timing, pregnancy, breastfeeding and medicine precautions.
  • Persistent or severe symptoms need reassessment rather than repeated self-treatment.

Frequently asked questions

Why does my partner need treatment without symptoms?

Silent infection is common. Treating only one person can leave the parasite circulating between partners.

Does a positive test prove a recent exposure?

No. Untreated infection can persist, so the result alone cannot date it or establish what happened in a relationship.

Can discharge colour confirm trichomoniasis?

No. Several conditions cause similar changes, and some infections cause no visible changes at all.

Is a negative microscope test enough?

Not always. A more sensitive test may be needed when concern remains.

Can I use a thrush cream instead?

No. It does not replace the prescribed oral treatment for this parasite.

When can we have sex again?

Wait until everyone has completed treatment, symptoms have resolved and the clinic’s waiting period has passed. NHS advice includes at least one week after everyone finishes.

Should I take a molecular test two weeks after treatment?

Discuss the reason for testing. CDC advises waiting at least three weeks after completion when a molecular test is used for persistent infection; contact the clinic earlier if you have symptoms.

Can I be treated during pregnancy?

Yes, with the appropriate medicine. Metronidazole is used when indicated; tinidazole should be avoided in pregnancy.

Does this infection mean I will become infertile?

No. Complications are possible but not inevitable. Timely assessment is especially important for pelvic pain or signs of another infection.

Can trichomoniasis return after successful treatment?

Yes. Treatment does not create immunity. Partner care and the recommended follow-up test help identify avoidable reinfection.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
